Claude.notes: Advanced framing and page architecture are clean, and each lesson anchors to a recognisable case (JPMorgan COIN, Apple Card, Netflix, Microsoft-Nadella). But cases are told as third-person success stories rather than problems the framework then solves, no protagonist arrives at the insight, and no AI-specific vocabulary is defined anywhere in a module aimed at leaders who must interrogate vendor claims. The 15-question Module Test is generic template filler — Q13 contains an unrendered '{course_title}' placeholder and distractors read 'S - Additional consideration or context-dependent factor'.
Claude.topIssue: Case studies are narrated as completed corporate wins with no protagonist and no discovery arc — the learner is told the takeaway rather than led to it, breaking the AESOP story→insight pattern.

Gemini.notes: No AI-specific vocabulary (LLM, model, hallucination, agent, RAG, fine-tuning, evaluation) is defined in a module that promises 'AI vendor evaluation' as an outcome. Case facts are loose: COIN launched 2017 not 2019, the Apple Card incident was Nov 2019 not 2020 and NYDFS ultimately found no unlawful discrimination, and Netflix's $1B and $50B figures are conflated. Frameworks (five risk categories, four value dimensions, five phases) are asserted with false precision when NIST AI RMF, ISO/IEC 42001, and the EU AI Act use different structures.
Gemini.topIssue: Zero AI-specific terms are defined in a module built to teach leaders to procure and govern AI systems — a leader cannot interrogate a vendor's technical claims after completing it.

Perplexity.notes: The module never mentions LLMs, generative AI, ChatGPT/Claude/Gemini/Copilot, agents, RAG, or foundation models — despite the intro claiming AI 'in three years moved from curiosity to essential utility'. All four case anchors predate the GenAI shift: JPMorgan COIN (2017), Apple Card (2019), Netflix (~2016 figures), Microsoft-Nadella cut off 'by 2023'. No reference to the EU AI Act (in force 2024), NIST AI RMF, ISO/IEC 42001, or SEC AI-washing enforcement — the actual regulatory landscape a 2026 leader must reason about.
Perplexity.topIssue: A 2026 AI leadership module with no mention of LLMs, generative AI, agents, EU AI Act enforcement, NIST AI RMF, or ISO/IEC 42001 is missing the entire vocabulary of the era it claims to prepare leaders for.

Claude.notes: Dated case anchors (Airbnb 2019, DeepMind 2020, Spotify 2021, Netflix 2006-2018) each give the lesson a memorable hook, but every story literally states the framework's answer before the concept section teaches it — so the concept becomes exposition rather than discovery. No protagonist carries across lessons; each vignette is a one-shot corporate anecdote. Lesson 4 quiz degrades into generic platitudes and the 15-question Module Test is the same broken template with '{course_title}' leaking into Q13.
Claude.topIssue: The case-study vignettes state the concept section's answer up front (three-pillar org, staged gates, ML platform), so the concept teaching becomes exposition of an already-revealed solution rather than a discovered insight.

Gemini.notes: Compensation numbers ('$300K+ senior ML engineer, $500K+ research scientist') are presented as universal facts with no geography, year, level, or source. The 60-70% / 40-50% / 80-90% gate pass rates, the 5-phase project lifecycle, the 4-stage maturity model, and the three-pillar DeepMind reorg with those exact team names are all stylised and un-sourced. MLOps, data drift, A/B testing framework, and model governance are used as jargon without being defined for the learner who most needs them explained. AlphaFold is attributed to a 2020 reorg though CASP14 was Nov 2020.
Gemini.topIssue: Quantitative benchmarks (comp bands, gate pass rates, 6-week feature deploy, 3-6 month applied cycle) are asserted as industry norms without any source, and terms like MLOps and data drift are named without being defined.

Perplexity.notes: All four case anchors predate the GenAI era (2019/2020/2021/2006-2018) and nothing addresses LLM-era team building — prompt engineers, evals engineers, red-team/AI-safety roles, agent engineers, fine-tuning specialists. Post-ChatGPT hiring dynamics and 2024-2026 frontier-lab comp escalation are absent. The 'ML Platform' story stops at Netflix 2017 with no reference to Databricks, Vertex AI, SageMaker, Weights & Biases, Ray, LangSmith, Bedrock, or Azure AI Foundry. Risk vocabulary omits agentic-system failures, prompt injection, jailbreaks, and model-provider deprecation.
Perplexity.topIssue: The ML-team taxonomy (data scientist / ML engineer / research scientist) predates the current split into ML platform, applied AI, GenAI product, evals, and safety roles that dominate 2025-2026 hiring.

Claude.notes: Clean four-lesson procurement arc (due diligence → assessment → contract → deployment) with vivid numeric anchors (customer concentration ≤15%, pilot 1-5%, phased 10-20% / 25-50%). Case studies are narrated as fait accompli — the Microsoft 95%→60% story concludes with the answer before the concept section introduces it, and the Goldman/Anthropic story asserts a completed contract negotiation without any dilemma for the learner. Module Test is the same 15-question generic filler with '{course_title}' leaking and 'S / T / R - Additional consideration…' distractors — it tests nothing about procurement.
Claude.topIssue: Every case vignette resolves the tension before the concept section arrives — learners watch a completed procurement rather than reasoning toward the framework, so the story→insight arc collapses.

Gemini.notes: 'California's SB-1001' is cited as an emerging AI regulation, but SB-1001 is the 2018 bot-disclosure law — an odd choice next to the EU AI Act. Prompt injection, model drift, and adversarial testing are named as AI-specific vulnerabilities but never defined. 'Vendors claimed 95% accuracy… dropped to 60% on legacy code' is stated without defining the accuracy metric (pass@1? functional correctness?), which is precisely the imprecision the lesson tells learners to guard against. The IP framing ('client-specific enhancements remain client property') is presented as a universal rule when it's heavily contested in practice.
Gemini.topIssue: SB-1001 (a 2018 bot-disclosure law) is miscited as emerging AI regulation, and prompt injection / model drift / adversarial testing are named as AI-specific risks but never defined — leaving learners unable to distinguish them from generic edge-case testing.

Perplexity.notes: All case studies are 2023-2024; nothing from 2025 or 2026 in a module dated April 2026. Misses the EU AI Act enforcement milestones that dominate 2026 procurement (GPAI obligations Aug 2025, high-risk Aug 2026), the NIST AI RMF GenAI Profile, and ISO/IEC 42001 certification. The current vendor landscape (OpenAI, Anthropic, Azure OpenAI, Bedrock, Cohere, Mistral, Databricks, Snowflake) appears only via a single mention of Anthropic. No mention of agentic-system procurement (tool-use permissions, MCP servers, autonomous action logging) or modern evaluation frameworks (HELM, MT-Bench, SWE-bench, τ-bench).
Perplexity.topIssue: California SB-1001 (the 2018 bot-disclosure law) is cited as an emerging AI regulation while the actual 2024-2026 California AI statutes (AB 2013 training-data transparency, SB 942 AI Transparency Act, SB 1047) are absent.

Claude.notes: Strongest story-problem match in the course sits in Lesson 1 — GM technicians' 'expertise devaluation' vignette precisely foreshadows the cognitive/emotional/social taxonomy the concept section then teaches. L3 (JPMorgan → competency-based training) also lands cleanly. But L2's Microsoft story surfaces top-performer resistance yet pivots to a generic Three Horizons + stakeholder-mapping framework that doesn't resolve the tension, and L4's Unilever story previews multi-metric evaluation but pivots to standard Kirkpatrick. Module Test is unusable filler with the '{course_title}' placeholder Q13 and 'S - Additional consideration…' distractors that reappear across the whole course.
Claude.topIssue: The Lesson 4 quiz and the 15-question Module Test ship as generic template items — several distractors read 'S - Additional consideration or context-dependent factor' and Q13 leaks an unrendered '{course_title}' variable, so the summative assessment measures nothing module-specific.

Gemini.notes: Every headline statistic (73% MIT-Sloan employee-monitoring stat, 3x future-role stat, McKinsey 2.8x adoption uplift, JPMorgan 89% user satisfaction / 6-months-to-8-weeks, Unilever 67%→94%) is stated without source URL, study title, or year. 'JPMorgan Chase's implementation of COIN in 2017 required retraining 3,000+ legal professionals' conflates the COIN automation narrative with a training program that has no matching public record. Kirkpatrick is billed as 'adapted for AI' but is presented in its standard four levels with AI-flavored parentheticals — no actual adaptation is shown. 'Unlike traditional software with clear if-then logic, AI systems…' misleads by implying deterministic software is transparent and ML is inherently opaque.
Gemini.topIssue: Every headline statistic used in the lessons (73% MIT-Sloan, 3x future-role, 2.8x McKinsey, 89% JPMorgan, 67%→94% Unilever) is asserted without citation, and the COIN 3,000-person retraining framing does not match public reporting of the automation story.

Perplexity.notes: All four flagship cases are from 2017-2020 — pre-ChatGPT AI deployments. The change-management challenges of 2025-2026 that a leader actually faces (shadow ChatGPT use, prompt-engineering skill gaps, GenAI copyright/data-leak exposure, agentic-workflow governance, tool-permission fatigue) never appear. No mention of LLMs, generative AI, copilots, agents, RAG, or foundation models. Cited research tops out at McKinsey 2023 — nothing after ChatGPT's third birthday. COIN is used as a marquee legal-AI example in 2026 when learners actually deal with Harvey, CoCounsel, Copilot for M365, and Claude for legal work.
Perplexity.topIssue: All four flagship case studies (GM 2018, Microsoft 2019, JPMorgan 2017, Unilever 2020) are pre-ChatGPT — the module addresses none of the shadow-AI, GenAI-adoption, or agent-governance change-management challenges that dominate 2026.

Claude.notes: Real, verifiable incidents (Bing Chat Feb 2023, UK A-level 2020, Apple Card, EU AI Act) anchor the module usefully, and lab prompts finally assign concrete executive personas (CRO, CLO) with multi-part deliverables. Lesson 3's story-concept coupling is weak: an A-level fairness incident (embedded historical bias in a statistical standardization) pivots into a model-drift/brittleness/monitoring taxonomy that doesn't actually explain what went wrong in the story. Module Test is again generic template content with placeholder distractors — the recurring shipwreck across every module in this course.
Claude.topIssue: Lesson 3's UK A-level story (a fairness incident driven by historical bias in a statistical standardization model) is used to introduce a model-drift/brittleness taxonomy that doesn't explain the story's actual failure mechanism.

Gemini.notes: The UK A-level 'algorithm' is described as an AI/ML failure; it was a rule-based statistical standardization model, not machine learning — a category error in a module titled AI Risk. Apple Card is dated to 2021 and framed as confirmed bias, but the NYDFS report (March 2021) actually found no unlawful discrimination — the module presents a contested outcome as settled. 'Value-at-risk models' and 'Monte Carlo simulation' are name-dropped as ways to quantify AI risk without any explanation of how they map to model failure modes. Algorithmic brittleness and adversarial-input failure are conflated in a single sentence.
Gemini.topIssue: The UK A-level standardization algorithm is described as an ML/AI failure in a module titled AI Risk — it was a rule-based statistical adjustment on historical data, not machine learning, which is a category error executive learners will absorb wholesale.

Perplexity.notes: The EU AI Act is still framed as a 'proposal' from May 2021 with implementation 'beginning in 2024' — in mid-2026 the Act is in force with GPAI obligations (Aug 2025) and high-risk obligations (Aug 2026) as the live dates. No mention of the NIST AI Risk Management Framework (1.0 Jan 2023, GenAI Profile Jul 2024) or ISO/IEC 42001 (Dec 2023) — both baseline for a 2026 executive audience. Bing 'Sydney' is a three-year-old incident; more recent executive-relevant failures (Air Canada chatbot liability 2024, DPD chatbot, Google AI Overviews, Grok content incidents) are absent. US regulatory discussion is stuck in 2023-2024 framing.
Perplexity.topIssue: The EU AI Act is described as a 'proposal' from May 2021 — in mid-2026 it's in force with GPAI (Aug 2025) and high-risk (Aug 2026) obligations live, and neither NIST AI RMF nor ISO/IEC 42001 is mentioned at all in a module about AI risk.

Claude.notes: L1's story-problem match is actually strong — the Wells Fargo Caremark framing sets up the fiduciary-oversight concept precisely, and the four-lesson arc (fiduciary duty → legal compliance → audit oversight → strategic integration) is well-scaffolded. But every case study in this module (Wells Fargo AI derivative suit, Babylon Health $12M FTC in March 2024, Goldman $200M AI trading loss with SEC investigation, Microsoft's 45%-of-comp AI-governance metric) appears to be fabricated or heavily embellished. In an executive-education module on board governance, that is disqualifying — any director who fact-checks a single case will lose trust in the whole. Module Test is the same broken template shipped across the course.
Claude.topIssue: The four flagship case studies (Wells Fargo Delaware AI derivative suit, Babylon Health FTC $12M FCRA March 2024, Goldman $200M AI-trading loss, Microsoft 45%-comp AI metric) do not appear in public record as described — fabricated case data is a credibility failure in a governance module.

Gemini.notes: Four of four case studies do not match public record: no Wells Fargo Delaware Chancery AI-oversight derivative suit with $3B AML at that scale, no Babylon Health FTC/FCRA $12M settlement in March 2024 (Babylon collapsed in 2023), no Goldman Sachs $200M AI-trading loss with SEC investigation as described, no Microsoft proxy tying 45% of executive comp to AI governance. Model drift, bias emergence, and explainability are named as monitoring/audit targets but not defined. Caremark and Marchand doctrine underlie L1's substantive reasoning but are never named — a learner can't research further. The EU AI Act is mentioned once without its risk-tier structure, which is exactly what a board needs to reason about materiality.
Gemini.topIssue: All four flagship case studies (Wells Fargo AI derivative suit, Babylon Health FTC $12M, Goldman $200M AI trading loss, Microsoft 45%-of-comp) appear to be fabricated or heavily embellished — a disqualifying factual failure in a governance module executive directors will fact-check.

Perplexity.notes: All four case anchors are dated 2023-early 2024 with no reference to 2025 developments a mid-2026 board-governance module should own: EU AI Act GPAI obligations coming into force (Aug 2025), US federal AI EO shifts, SEC AI-washing enforcement actions, NIST AI RMF Generative AI Profile, ISO/IEC 42001 AI management system certification. No generative-AI-specific board risks that dominate 2025-2026 discourse — agentic AI liability, model-provider concentration risk, IP/training-data litigation exposure (NYT v. OpenAI), shareholder proposals on AI transparency. State-level AI legislation is referenced generically without naming Colorado SB 24-205, California SB 1047, or NYC Local Law 144. Babylon Health is used as a 2024 exemplar despite the company collapsing in 2023.
Perplexity.topIssue: Babylon Health is cited as a 2024 FTC/FCRA exemplar for board oversight, but Babylon collapsed into administration in 2023 — any 2026 learner who fact-checks the anchor case will find it broken.

modules.module: M9: From Consumer to Builder: Leading AI Creation

Claude.notes: Best module in the set on capability delta — L3's six-part commissioning brief (problem, success metrics, scope, constraints, timeline, team structure) is a template a leader could copy into a real project doc tomorrow, and the lesson kicker 'Module 9 · Lesson N' provides the orientation the rest of the course lacks. L1 and L3 story-concept matches are tight. But every 'case' is an anonymized composite ('a CEO', 'a VP of Marketing', 'a major retailer'), so there is no verifiable anchor and no continuing character — L2 is a success-story vignette that doesn't pose the problem the concept section then solves.
Claude.topIssue: Every case study is an anonymized archetype with no company, name, or date — the module gives learners no verifiable anchors and no continuing character to travel with.

Gemini.notes: 'Custom GPTs: You can create custom versions of large language models trained on your data' is a substantive misconception — OpenAI's Custom GPTs do not train the underlying model; they combine a system prompt with retrieval and (optionally) tools. The 'about 70% of AI project failures are data-related' claim is asserted without citation. Every 'case' is an anonymized composite so nothing can be verified. Explainability is framed as a no-code-specific problem when it's a general property of most ML systems, and no mention is made of regulated-lending adverse-action-notice requirements. The lifecycle described (data prep → train → evaluate → deploy → monitor) reads as pre-2022 supervised-model vocabulary — no fine-tuning vs. prompting distinction, no RAG, no evals-as-code, no agentic pattern.
Gemini.topIssue: 'Custom GPTs create custom versions of large language models trained on your data' misdescribes how Custom GPTs work — they use a system prompt plus RAG, not model training — a substantive AI misconception in a course teaching leaders to commission AI systems.

Perplexity.notes: Only two LLMs are named (Claude and GPT) and 'custom GPTs' is the only named build pattern — no mention of agents, MCP, tool use, evals, guardrails frameworks, model routing, or on-device models, which are mainstream 2025-2026 leadership vocabulary. The retailer inventory example is a thinly veiled COVID-era anecdote (supply-chain shocks, two years of training data) with no acknowledgement of more recent, executive-relevant AI incidents (2024-2025 agent failures, public post-mortems, model-provider deprecations). Vendor-governance language (audit rights, milestone-based payment) never references the EU AI Act, NIST AI RMF, or ISO/IEC 42001. 'Prompt engineering' is presented as the primary lever for governing LLM behavior without mention of system-level guardrails, evals, or output filtering that are now standard.
Perplexity.topIssue: The module's build vocabulary is pre-2024: only Claude and GPT are named, and there is no reference to agents, MCP, tool use, evals, guardrails, or the EU AI Act / NIST AI RMF / ISO/IEC 42001 that a 2026 leader learning to commission AI would expect to see.
